stem.text: Find the particular solution of the differential equation

points.text: 5m2 + 4m + 1 = 0 ⇒ m = –2/5 ± (1/5)i; auxiliary equation. M1 for correct type of roots a±bi
y = e–2x/5(Acos(1/5)x + Bsin(1/5)x) + x2 – x – 5; general solution, must have 'y=', FT on CF
y′ = e–2x/5(–(1/5)Asin(1/5)x + (1/5)Bcos(1/5)x) – (2/5)e–2x/5(Acos(1/5)x + Bsin(1/5)x) + 2x – 1; differentiates. General solution must be of the correct form, must use product rule
0 = A–5; 0 = (1/5)B–(2/5)A–1 ⇒ A=5, B=15; uses initial conditions. A1 is both A and B correct

markScheme.note: This MS uses M/A/B/DM/DB mark codes, not the biology-style ;/A/R/I shorthand.

explanation.text: This is a second-order linear ODE with constant coefficients and a polynomial forcing term. The general solution is complementary function (from the auxiliary equation) plus a particular integral (matching the form of the RHS, here a quadratic since the RHS is quadratic).
The auxiliary equation 5m²+4m+1=0 has discriminant 16–20=–4 < 0, giving complex roots a±bi, which produce an oscillating, exponentially-decaying complementary function e^{ax}(Acos bx + Bsin bx).

reasoningChain: Write the auxiliary equation 5m²+4m+1=0 and solve for m using the quadratic formula, getting complex roots.
Write the complementary function in the e^{ax}(Acosbx+Bsinbx) form matching those roots.
Since the RHS is a quadratic (x²+7x+1), try a quadratic particular integral y=px²+qx+r.
Substitute y, y′, y″ into the original ODE and equate coefficients of x², x¹, x⁰ to solve for p, q, r.
Combine the complementary function and particular integral into the general solution.
Differentiate the general solution once (needs the product rule on the exponential-times-trig term).
Use the two initial conditions y(0)=0 and y′(0)=0 to form two equations and solve for A and B.
Write the final particular solution with the found A, B values.

inferredMistakes.text: Trying a particular integral of the wrong degree (e.g. just y=px+q, missing the x² term), since the RHS is quadratic and the particular integral must match that degree.

Forgetting the product rule when differentiating the complementary function (which is a product of an exponential and a trig sum), and instead just differentiating the trig part while leaving the exponential factor unchanged.
Using only one initial condition (e.g. just y(0)=0) to try to find both A and B, when two independent conditions are needed since there are two unknown constants.
